entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Theoderich von Wied (c. 1170 – April 3, 1242) served as Archbishop of Trier and Prince-Elector of the Holy Roman Empire from 1212 until his death, positioning him as a pivotal ecclesiastical and political figure within the fragmented yet powerful German territories of the High Middle Ages. His long episcopate was characterized by a delicate balance of spiritual leadership, territorial expansion, and active engagement in imperial politics, notably as a staunch supporter of Emperor Frederick II Hohenstaufen. His influence extended beyond his archdiocese, shaping the religious landscape and political machinations of the Rhineland and the wider empire during a period of intense papal-imperial conflict.

During his tenure, Theoderich significantly expanded the temporal power of the Archbishopric of Trier, acquiring numerous castles and territories, thereby solidifying its position as one of the most important prince-bishoprics. He actively participated in several imperial diets and played a crucial role in the election of Frederick II as Holy Roman Emperor in 1212, subsequently becoming one of Frederick's most reliable allies. Theoderich also fostered religious life, founding the Cistercian Himmerod Abbey and supporting other monastic institutions. He embarked on crusading ventures, participating in the Fifth Crusade (1217–1221) and later promoting the Livonian Crusade, demonstrating the dual secular and spiritual responsibilities of a medieval prince-bishop.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Theoderich von Wied's three-decade tenure as Archbishop of Trier significantly strengthened one of the Holy Roman Empire's most important prince-bishoprics, laying groundwork for its continued political and ecclesiastical influence. His unwavering support for Emperor Frederick II also played a crucial role in imperial politics during a tumultuous era.
